Fast Multi-Target Circular Barcode Pose Tracking

Part V of a 10 year project designed for better optical localization. In this notebook we

  • Match multiple circular barcodes in the scene
  • Decode them so each has an unambiguous code for matching
  • Compile into WASM via AssemblyScript for instantly fast performance
  • Use Web Workers for parallelism
  • Fuse multiple barcodes to get a pose

Less than 2ms per frame on Macbook, 12ms on phone 🤙

⠿➕edit

The Scanner

This lets you run the barcode matcher a few ways

  • wave your mobile displaying the pattern infront of your webcam on a laptop running this notebook

  • print out the pattern on paper and track with this notebook on your mobile

  • connect Claude Code to the notebook live on your Laptop and let it drive and take measurements (also `/remote-control` from Claude Code from mobile)

  • download the notebook as a single file and let Claude Code choose how to edit and run it

About

There are a few optical trackers, including circular barcodes. The unique thing about this one is the design around single scan lines, so barcodes can be recognized with appropriate hardware as pixels leave the camera's MPI. This is potentially hundreds of times faster than the frames per second rating of a camera. This notebook is just about the single frame recognition algorithm.

§1 The barcode mark

⠿➕edit
⠿➕edit
download man 45 (60mm)
radius →  centre to rim
id 45  =  bits 101101
8 mid edges — one per cell, always 3 cell boundaries
11 edges to position against on this scan line
⠿➕edit

A circular barcode is a set of concentric rings. With Manchester Encoding of 6 bits, every bit has at least one intensity change (an edge). These edges can help position the barcode ion a scan line and also double as a digital label.

⠿➕edit

§2 Multiple Barcodes

If the layout of the barcodes is known, their combination gives a homography estimate. There is no matching ambiguity because the barcodes label themselves.

⠿➕edit
download A4 target
7 marks, ids 56, 11, 22, 29, 37, 46, 51 — the seven non-zero codewords of a [6,3] code, so no single misread cell can turn one member into another.
48mm marks, 69.6mm pitch, cluster rotated 30°, sheet 187.2 × 168.55mm on A4. Tightest clearance between marks that can share a scan row: 21.6mm (2.14× the dark disc it has to beat).
The rotation is not decoration — it is worth more than the pitch is. Over three poses each, rotated reads 7/7/7 marks against 3/3/3 upright at this pitch. Why is not established: the obvious explanations (collinear triples, along-row clearance) are both contradicted by the same table, so this is an empirical setting, not a derived one.
Working distance: a mark needs roughly 4 pixels per tooth, so keep the whole cluster in frame with each mark above ~60px. On a 1280-wide camera that is roughly 0.4–1.2 m from the sheet.
Print at 100%, not "fit to page" — the millimetre geometry is the calibration. Measure the 100mm bar to check.

§3.1 The label set

§4 Detection
§4.1 The circular encoding
§4.2 One scanline
§4.3 Frame fusion
§4.4 The plane

The mark is designed so it is easy to recognize and localize from a single scan line of pixels. The encoding gives it a label and edges for sharp positioning.

⠿➕edit

§4.1 The circular barcode pattern

⠿➕edit
⠿➕edit
⠿➕edit

A scan row cuts every ring twice, and one projective map on that row carries each ring's first crossing to its second — the same map for every ring, because they are concentric. That map is an involution: it is its own inverse, so applying it twice returns the point you started from. Two points on the row are left alone by it — PPP, where the row passes closest to the mark's centre, and QQQ, the vanishing point of the row's direction. Those two fixed points are all it takes to undo the perspective along that row.

The key coordinate is u=r2u = r^2u=r2. After normalising by the involution's fixed points, t=(x−P)/(x−Q)t = (x-P)/(x-Q)t=(x−P)/(x−Q) gives t=ckt = c kt=ck exactly, so

u:=t2=c2(r2−d2)=Ar2+B.u := t^2 = c^2(r^2 - d^2) = A r^2 + B.u:=t2=c2(r2−d2)=Ar2+B.

The whole per-row warp — chord offset and perspective together — collapses to an affine map in r2r^2r2-space. A code built from affine-recognisable structure in that space is detectable on every row, at every pose, from every edge, and no part of it needs to be reserved for finding the mark rather than reading it.

§4.2 One scanline

One scanline is enough to determine 3 of the 6 position/orientation degrees of freedom for the barcode in 3D space.

barcode on line geometric
center position along line x offset
width on line z offset
yaw rotation around y

3 scanlines on the same barcode can retreive a homography (5DOF), and if the size of the barcode is fixed and the camera field of view known, all 6 (albiet some of them are pretty noisy).

The first step to towards pose retreival is edge detection

After edge detection, adjacent edges are grouped. Barcode geometry bounds the problem space.

⠿➕edit
⠿➕edit

surving groups have a clear involution around a reflection point P, a very distinctive pattern stemming from the properties of an orientated set of concentric rings, that is preserved even if the scanline is off-center to the barcode.

⠿➕edit
⠿➕edit

Once P is cracked the slope is a fit and the barcode can be fully read if all its edges are observable. It is probably true that some of the bits of the barcode can be decoded even if the scan is off-center, but not tried here.

§4.5 Making it fast

The problem is parrelizable at the scan line level. In this notebook we farm out the work to web workers to make use of multi-core computation available on laptops and mobiles.

§4.7 Relabelling

The bank's reference truth labels (§3.1) are computed by a more comprehensive version of the tracker.

  1. The edge threshold is chosen per frame.
  2. The plane is fitted by exhaustive RANSAC over the 4-subsets, not by dropping the worst point. A mark decoded under the wrong id sits perfectly on its own ink and a whole pitch from where that id belongs, and with seven points it drags a least-squares fit far enough that the innocent marks look as guilty as it does.
  3. The plane may flag a measurement, never quietly replace one. Four points fit a homography exactly, so a 4-inlier consensus at rms 0 is not evidence of anything; five is the first count that can be contradicted. Even then a hand-held sheet at a grazing angle is not planar to 4px, so a measurement is overruled only at a residual on the order of the mark spacing — paper curl moves a mark a few px, a misread sits a whole pitch away — or when the pixel contrast of the mark's own printed design refuses it as well.

One frame at a time below. Everything it reports about a mark is evidence from a different instrument: dirs is how many directions saw it, line rms how well their lines met, plane px its residual against the plane the other marks determine, contrast the collar-minus-core of its own ink, and moved px how far the result sits from the label this notebook currently ships.

Claude Code Pairing


Bridges a lopecode notebook to Claude Code via WebSocket.


Claude Code CLI  ←MCP→  Channel Server  ←WS→  This Module (browser)

Cell groups (in dependency order):


    

  1. UI — cc_chat (main interface), cc_watch_table (variable inspector)
    2. 

  2. State — cc_config, cc_notebook_id, cc_activity, cc_status, cc_messages, cc_watches, cc_module, voiceEnabled
    3. 

  3. Module lookup — cc_find_module resolves module names via runtime.mains
    4. 

  4. Serialization — cc_serialize_value (safe value→string for transport)
    5. 

  5. Variable watcher — cc_watchers observes variables, debounces & sends updates
    6. 

  6. Command handlers — cc_handle_* (one per MCP tool)
    7. 

  7. Command dispatch — cc_command_handlers routes action→handler
    8. 

  8. WebSocket — cc_ws manages connect/pair/auto-reconnect and message dispatch
    9. 

  9. Side effects — cc_change_forwarder streams cell edits, cc_voice optional speech I/O
    10. 

  10. Imports — currentModules, exportToHTML, compile, history, runtime-sdk helpers
    11. 


    

    

      
⠿➕edit

Reactive Inputs.input() cells holding connection state. These are the shared mutable atoms that UI and WebSocket cells read/write.

Module lookup & serialization


cc_find_module resolves a module name (e.g. "@tomlarkworthy/exporter-3") to a runtime Module object by polling viewof currentModules.value at call time (not reactively). cc_serialize_value safely converts any runtime value to a truncated string for transport.

    

    

      
⠿➕edit

    


    

  
cc_find_module = ƒ(runtime, moduleName)

    

    

      
⠿➕edit

    


    

  
cc_serialize_value = ƒ(value, maxLen)

    

    

      
⠿➕edit

    


    

  


Variable watcher


Subscribes to Observable variables via observe(), debounces updates (1s), and forwards changes to Claude Code over the WebSocket. Also maintains the cc_watches table UI.

    

    

      
⠿➕edit

    


    

  
cc_watchers = Object {watchVariable: ƒ(runtime, name, moduleName), unwatchVariable: ƒ(name, moduleName), unwatchAll: ƒ(), setSend: ƒ(fn)}

    

    

      
⠿➕edit

    


    

  


Command handlers


One handler per MCP tool. Each receives a cmd object and the Observable runtime, returns {ok, result} or {ok:false, error}. Handlers: get-variable, define-variable, define-cell, delete-variable, list-variables, list-cells, run-tests, create-module, delete-module, eval, fork, watch, unwatch.

Command dispatch & WebSocket


cc_command_handlers maps action strings to handler functions. cc_ws manages the WebSocket lifecycle: connect, pair with token, dispatch incoming messages (commands, replies, tool-activity), and auto-reconnect from the URL hash cc= param or sessionStorage.

cc_change_forwarder polls the local-change-history and streams new cell edits to Claude Code. cc_voice provides optional speech recognition input and TTS output for hands-free pairing.
